_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: He may not say: I will separate ten: the lean ones, and the rest are exempt, because only five would remain, and those are not subject to tithing [being fewer than ten].
rashi:a1.2: Rather, he brings them into the pen: all of them, lean and fat alike. Two things are taught here: first, that he cannot pick out the lean ones; second, that although only five remain, he cannot say they are entirely exempt; rather, they combine with another gathering time. It seems to me that this did not need to be said, since we said above (57b) that five before the gathering time and five after it combine to make ten. Rather, this is its meaning: he may not say, etc., “and let the rest be exempt now,” meaning: I will not bring them into the pen with the others, and although the gathering time has arrived I may sell them and slaughter them, since they are not subject to tithing, as the gathering time fixes [the obligation] only for something fit to be tithed, and these five are not. Rather, he brings them all into the pen together and takes out ten, and the rest combine with another gathering time perforce, since they were fixed for tithe in the pen, and he may not sell or slaughter them.
rashi:a3.1: At the Festival: on the Shabbat before the Festival, when the laws of the Festival are expounded.
rashi:a3.2: And this one: which remained last makes a tally fit [to reach ten] both here and there, and exempts them all; and it itself is sacred, whether it went out or remained last, since the tenth is sanctified of its own accord.
rashi:a4.1: He called one from the start: he did not call it tenth but began counting again as at first, one, two, three; so the nineteenth turns out to be the tenth, and even the nine he counted at first were exempted by a tally fit [to reach ten].
rashi:a4.2: Of its own accord it is sacred: even though he called it one; so the last nine would not be exempt.
rashi:a5.1: Pair by pair: two as one, and the tenth “pair” was only a single animal, so all of them would be exempted by a fit tally, since that last one is fit for here and for there.
rashi:a5.2: According to the number of animals: we do not follow what his mouth says, “one, two,” but the animals he took out. Once he has taken out five pairs, which are ten animals, one of them is sacred; and all those he takes out afterward, by what would they be exempt? They are not a tally fit [to reach ten].
rashi:a6.1: Fortunate is the mother of Rav Huna bar Seḥora, who explained it to Rava in line with his own teaching: that is, the mother of Rav Huna bar Seḥora merited to bear a son like him, who knew how to resolve Rava’s teaching in the middle of the discourse, and resolved it along the lines of Rava’s own teaching; for Rava said above that a tally fit [to reach ten] exempts, and this is how Rav Huna resolves it here: that one is fit for here and fit for there.
rashi:a7.1: MISHNA. The ninth and tenth are flawed: that is, the one he called ninth, which is really the tenth, and the one he called tenth, which is really the eleventh, stand to be spoiled, because he thinks the [so-called] ninth is non-sacred and the [so-called] tenth is the tithe; and if he acted so without consulting the court, they are spoiled. [The correct ruling is] as the latter clause teaches: if he called the tenth ninth and the eleventh tenth, the tenth is tithe and the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering. Another explanation: they are flawed because no sanctity takes hold of them to be sacrificed, and they are eaten in their blemished state. For although elsewhere, if he called the tenth ninth and the eleventh tenth, the tenth is sacrificed as tithe and the eleventh as a peace offering, as below, that applies only where he erred from the ninth onward; but here the whole count above the ninth is wrong, for he called the eighth seventh and the seventh sixth, or the ninth eighth, so the tenth and eleventh are not sacred to be sacrificed, since he erred so much. And when the mishna teaches “two emerged as one,” it is not speaking of the ninth and tenth, since Rava sets out the law from the ninth onward in the Gemara (60b); rather it speaks of one who erred in the count before the ninth, for example two emerged at the eighth and he called them eighth, or two emerged at the seventh and he called them seventh. And what is taught below, “if he counted them backward, the tenth is sacred,” is for the reason given there, citing the Persian counting, which calls ten “one.” Some explain that they are flawed because the case is where he intended to count them as one; and in tractate Nazir, in the chapter Beit Shammai (Nazir 32a), we say regarding tithe: his mistake [sanctifies], but not his intention. But this is not convincing: for if so, even if he called the ninth tenth it should be flawed, without two emerging as one; and further, according to the one who disputes there and says “his mistake, and even his intention,” what can be said? And in my teacher’s notes I found that “flawed” means that sanctity takes hold of them, and he was unsure why the mishna used the word “flawed.” This is more convincing, and one can say that the mishna itself explains why they are flawed: because he called the ninth tenth, etc.
tosafot:a7.1: If two emerged as one, he counts them as two, and if he counted them as one, the ninth and tenth are flawed: Rashi explained: for example, two emerged when he reached six or seven and he counted them as one, and therefore he called the tenth, by the number of animals, ninth, and the eleventh tenth. Although just below it says that if he called the tenth ninth and the eleventh tenth, the tenth is tithe and the eleventh a peace offering, here they are flawed because he counted the two that emerged together as one, and we are unsure whether they become as one by his counting them as one or not. And although there is an opinion in the Gemara that the tenth according to the number of animals is sacred, the fact that he counted them as one makes it a doubt: the one called ninth is perhaps the ninth, perhaps the tenth, and the one called tenth is perhaps the tenth, perhaps [the eleventh,] sacred to be sacrificed.
gershom:a1.1: And the rest are exempt: from being combined [with a later gathering], even though he brought them all into the pen.
gershom:a2.1: At the Festival: on the Shabbat before the Festival, when they expound. For this one, the nineteenth, that remained in the pen, is fit to complete [the tally] here and there, and we say that [animals that went out in] a tally possibly fit [to reach ten] are exempt. And let him answer: even in a pen with one opening, where he counted nine, and when the tenth arrived he called that tenth one, from the start, and counted up to ten; now both the first nine and the last nine went out in a fit tally.
gershom:a3.1: He holds: Rav Huna; that is why he could not answer that way, because [by calling the tenth one] he did nothing, since the tenth is sanctified as tithe of its own accord even if he did not call it tenth, and the nine that remain have no fit tally and must combine with another gathering time. But with two openings, where nine go out here and nine there and one remains, it is certainly fit to complete [the tally] here and there.
gershom:a4.1: And let him answer: with one opening, where he counted them pair by pair, two as one, until he reached nine, which are eighteen, and he took out the one that remained and called it tenth, to exempt these nine and those nine.
gershom:a6.1: The tenth according to the number of animals is sacred, and not according to the counter’s reckoning: that is, we do not follow his own count, counting them pair by pair; rather, once five pairs have gone out, those are ten animals and one of them is sacred, and the other four pairs have no fit tally and would not be exempt. Therefore one cannot answer that way.
gershom:a7.1: Fortunate is the mother of Rav Huna bar Seḥora: for although he was not so great a scholar, he resolved the baraita for Rava at the Festival before the public, and he aimed well when he resolved it in line with Rava’s own teaching, who said that a fit tally exempts.
gershom:a8.1: He counted them as one, those two: the ninth and tenth are flawed, for the [so-called] ninth is the tenth and the [so-called] tenth is the eleventh, a peace offering, and peace offering and tithe are intermingled with each other, and they are not eaten [except] in their blemished state. For from a peace offering the breast and thigh go to the priests, while from the tithe there is no breast and thigh for the priests, only the sacrificial portions for the altar. If he gives breast and thigh from it to the priests, he brings sacrificial animals to disqualification, for perhaps the priests would not be counted to eat it, since they have other offerings, and they would leave it beyond its time, and so it comes to disqualification, whereas the breast and thigh of a tithe are certainly permitted to an Israelite. Therefore they have no remedy except that both graze until they become blemished, and the one that is the peace offering is redeemed with money, and afterward they are all eaten by Israelites.
rashi:a8.1: Is sacrificed as a peace offering: in the Gemara it is derived from a verse.
gershom:a17.1: The ninth is eaten in its blemished state: when it develops a blemish, since he called it by the name tithe; but it is not a full tithe, fit to be sacrificed, since it is the ninth; rather it is eaten in its blemished state.
gershom:a18.1: And the tenth is tithe, and is fit to be sacrificed, even though he called it ninth, for the tenth is certainly sacred of its own accord.
gershom:a19.1: And the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering: since the tenth is certainly sacred, that one is a peace offering. Further, this eleventh is sacred for this reason: since the name tenth was removed from the tenth, which was called ninth, and the eleventh was called tenth, therefore the sanctity of a peace offering takes hold of it, once the tenth is certainly sacred. And it renders a substitute: if he exchanged another animal for that eleventh, it is caught up as a substitute.
rashi:a9.1: And is there a substitute [that renders a substitute]? For the eleventh, which he called tenth, is the substitute of the tithe, and in tractate Temura (13a) we derive that a substitute does not render a substitute, as it is written “its substitute,” and not the substitute of its substitute.
gershom:a20.1: And does a substitute render a substitute? That is, this eleventh is itself the substitute of the tithe, as the Gemara says (60b): a mistake in tithe is a substitute; so how can it render a substitute? Is it not so that one does not substitute and then substitute again?
rashi:a9.2: If it were a substitute: that eleventh would not be sacrificed, since the substitute of a tithe is not sacrificed, as we derive in tractate Temura (5b) [tithe from the firstborn, through the shared word “passing”; and of the firstborn we expound: they are sacrificed, but their substitute is not]. Rather, certainly, since it is sacrificed as a peace offering, we regard it as an originally consecrated animal, and therefore it renders a substitute like any other peace offering.
gershom:a21.1: They said in the name of Rabbi Meir: if it were a substitute it would not be sacrificed. That is, certainly a substitute does not render a substitute; but here this eleventh is not a substitute, as it is not like other substitutes; rather, the name tithe was called upon it, and so it is sacrificed. If it were a substitute of the body of the tithe, in the manner of other substitutes, it would not be sacrificed; for we read in the first chapter of tractate Temura: “The Sages taught: ‘He shall not inquire’ …” until “Rabbi says: Why was tithe singled out? To judge it with regard to the substitute of its name and the substitute of its body, to tell you that the substitute of its name is sacrificed and the substitute of its body is not.” And this eleventh is a substitute of its name, and therefore it is sacrificed and renders a substitute, for it is not like other substitutes, which are substitutes of the body.
rashi:a9.3: From it: from the tenth itself.
rashi:a10.1: Kinteran: by hundreds, counting each hundred together.
gershom:a9.1: He counted them pair by pair, and when he reached the tenth pair he took the two as tithe.
gershom:a10.1: Kinteran: he counts by the hundred and takes ten out of a hundred.
rashi:a11.1: According to his number it is sacred: the count of ten that he is counting; once he has counted nine hundreds, the tenth hundred is sacred.
gershom:a11.1: It is sacred according to his number: as he counts them.
rashi:a11.2: According to the number of animals: we do not follow his own count; rather, once he has counted five pairs of animals, which are ten animals, [the tenth animal] is immediately tithe, by the animals’ count.
gershom:a12.1: According to the number of animals, as we said.
rashi:a13.1: And the tenth he calls tenth: this “he calls it” is not meant literally; rather it means: why are they flawed? You said that the ninth by the number of animals is the ninth and the tenth is the tenth, since we pay no attention to his own count; and since we pay no attention to it, why should the eleventh, which he calls tenth, and the tenth, which he calls ninth, be flawed? Let the eleventh be a peace offering and the tenth tithe.
gershom:a13.1: But according to the one who says it is sacred according to the number of animals, why are they flawed? If so, it is as though he called the certain ninth ninth and the certain tenth tenth.
gershom:a14.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: he answers according to Rav Kahana: when I said it is sacred according to the number of animals, that is where he intended to take them all out pair by pair, or by hundreds; but here in the mishna, where it emerged by itself, as it teaches “two emerged as one” of their own accord, it is sacred not according to the number of animals but according to his own count.
rashi:a14.1: Where it emerged by itself, not: we do not say it is sacred according to the number of animals; rather we follow his own count too.
rashi:a15.1: He counted them backward: he called the first to go out ten, the second nine, the third eight, and so on for all of them down to one; the tenth in the count, which he called one, is sacred.
gershom:a15.1: He counted them backward: to the first he called ten, to the second nine, down to one.
gershom:a16.1: Since it is in the Persian count, where they call ten “one,” this “one” is like the tenth by his own count, and is sacred. [The notes that follow] belong to the mishna, “the three of them are sacred,” which does not speak of animals that became intermingled.
rashi:b2.1: And all the tithe of the herd or the flock: this implies both where he called it tenth and where it was tenth in the count and he did not call it tenth.
rashi:b2.2: Eighth and twelfth: if he called them tenth.
gershom:b1.1: And all the tithe: to include anything upon which he called the name tithe.
gershom:b2.1: Even the eighth and twelfth: if he called the eighth tithe, and the twelfth.
rashi:b3.1: Just as it: the full tenth is sanctified only [when it is] close to it, for nothing is closer to it than itself.
rashi:b3.2: So too its mistake: the one about which he erred and called it tenth is sanctified only if he erred about one adjacent to the full tithe, such as the ninth and eleventh, which are adjacent to it, one before it and one after it.
gershom:b3.1: And its mistake sanctifies: for example, when he called the ninth tenth or the eleventh tenth.
gershom:b4.1: Just as it is sanctified only [when] close: that is, the tenth itself, when he calls it tenth; there is nothing closer than itself.
gershom:b5.1: So too its mistake is sanctified only [when] close to it: to exclude the eighth and twelfth.
rashi:b4.1: Unique: for the tenth is only one.
rashi:b4.2: So too its mistake is unique: if he erred with the ninth and the eleventh, the two would not be sanctified, only one of them; so how did you say that all of them are sanctified?
gershom:b6.1: So too its mistake is unique: that is, it sanctifies only one, either the ninth or the eleventh. And he raises an objection from the mishna, which teaches “the three of them are sacred,” which means two mistakes.
gershom:b7.1: Whose is this? The one that requires its mistake to be unique: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, as it is taught: “Never,” etc.
rashi:b5.1: Until he is silent at the ninth: for if he had called it tenth, the eleventh would not be sacred, since two mistakes for one tithe are not sacred, as its mistake is unique, like itself.
tosafot:b5.1: Until he is silent at the ninth (that is, he did not call it tenth): this can be explained in two ways. [First:] “until he is silent at the ninth” is not meant literally; it means he did not call it tenth, even if he called it ninth. For if he called it tenth, the eleventh is not sacred, since two mistakes are not sanctified together, as we require that its mistake be unique, like itself. Or one can explain further: if he called the ninth “ninth,” then it is no longer a mistake when he calls the tenth “ninth,” and it is as though he called it tenth, and the eleventh is not sanctified, since it does not count as though the name tenth were removed from it. On this reading “he is silent” is literal: he did not speak at all. This resolves a difficulty further on in our passage, where it says: “Here we are dealing with a case where one of them went ahead and put out its head, and he called it eleventh,” and asks: “In accordance with whom? Not in accordance with Rabbi, for Rabbi said that [calling it] eleventh is not a removal.” Then let it be explained where he called the one that put out its head “ninth,” which according to all is a removal! According to this explanation it is well, since that is not a removal, as we explained. And according to the first version that I explained, it is not explained as a case where he called it ninth because that would not need to be taught, since it is certainly a removal; but this needed to be taught, because at times, according to Rabbi, it is not a removal, where he has many animals.
gershom:b8.1: Until he is silent at the ninth: so that he does not call it by the name tenth, and he calls the tenth ninth and the eleventh tenth, so that there is only one mistake, the eleventh [called] tenth.
gershom:b9.1: [Calling the] tenth “ninth” is not a mistake, since the tenth is sacred of its own accord. And if you ask: then let him say likewise that if he was silent at the eleventh and did not call it tenth, [but] called the ninth tenth, that ninth should be sacred, since it is a single mistake. This is no difficulty: by right the eleventh is sacred, since the tenth itself has already become sacred, so this eleventh is a substitute of the name of the tithe, and it is caught up in the sanctity. But the ninth, when the tithe itself has not yet become sacred, how could [the tithe] catch the ninth and sanctify it, when it itself is not yet sacred? Therefore he spoke of the eleventh and not the ninth.
rashi:b6.1: And the reason of Rabbi Elazar is this: because he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who says in the mishna that a mistake [in tithe is a substitute], as he says, “and does a substitute render a substitute?”; and Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Elazar’s father, said in the first chapter of Temura (9a) that one does not substitute and then substitute again: once a substitute has been made for the animal one time, it no longer takes a substitute another time. So too here, there are not two mistakes for one tithe.
gershom:b10.1: And Rabbi Elazar holds like his father, Rabbi Shimon, who says in Temura that one does not substitute and then substitute again: after he has substituted a non-sacred animal for a consecrated animal, he does not again substitute another non-sacred animal for that same consecrated animal.
gershom:b11.1: So too here, the ninth and the eleventh are not [both] substituted for the tenth. And it stands to reason that this follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said there: just as one does not substitute two for one, so one does not substitute and then substitute again.
rashi:b7.1: At the ninth: when the ninth was due to come out.
rashi:b7.2: Tenth and non-sacred: for one of them is the ninth and one is the tithe, although he called it ninth.
rashi:b7.3: Intermingled: and they are eaten only in their blemished state; and one who shears or works one of them does not receive the forty [lashes], since perhaps it is the non-sacred one.
gershom:b12.1: The tenth and non-sacred are intermingled with each other: and both are eaten by the owners in their blemished state. That is why he says “tenth and non-sacred are intermingled”: if he shore or worked one of them, or ate one of them without a blemish, or redeemed or sold one of them, we do not flog him, out of doubt, since one of them is non-sacred.
gershom:b13.1: The tenth is sacred of its own accord: even though he did not call it tenth.
gershom:b14.1: And the ninth he calls tenth: since two emerged as one and he does not know which is the tenth and which the ninth, the tenth and ninth are intermingled with each other, and both are sacred; if he redeemed or sold one of them he is flogged, since he called both of them tenth; and they are eaten by the owners in their blemished state.
rashi:b9.1: The tenth and eleventh are intermingled: that is, a full tithe and a sacred eleventh are intermingled together; and since the eleventh, which is sacred, is sacrificed as a peace offering, both are sacrificed and eaten according to the stricter of the two: they require two placements [of blood] and the lifting of the breast and thigh, like a peace offering.
tosafot:b9.1: Two at the tenth, etc.: above, in chapter 2 (Bekhorot 17b, s.v. “efshar”), I explained that he could hold that it is impossible to be precise [so that two animals cannot emerge at exactly the same moment].
gershom:b15.1: The tenth and eleventh are intermingled with each other: for the eleventh is fit to be sacrificed as a peace offering, and the other is eaten by the owners in its blemished state. So now both graze until they become blemished, then he redeems one of them on account of the peace offering, and both are eaten by the owners in their blemished state.
gershom:b16.1: The tenth and non-sacred are intermingled: and both are eaten by the owners in their blemished state, without any redemption.
rashi:b10.1: Why do I need this additional case? Since he taught us that two emerged at the ninth and he called them tenth, I would know by itself that the same law applies where both emerged at the tenth.
gershom:b17.1: This is identical: “the tenth and eleventh are intermingled” is the same as “the tenth and ninth are intermingled,” and from one we learn the other.
gershom:b18.1: This teaches us: this, “the tenth and eleventh are intermingled,” [teaches] that whenever they emerge at the same time and he called them tenth, both are sacred, and one is sacrificed as a peace offering, even though the name tenth was not removed from the tenth, since he called it tenth.
rashi:b11.1: At the same time: where he called the name tenth upon the tenth and the eleventh at the same time, even though it was not removed, since he called the tenth too “tenth.”
gershom:b19.1: This statement, that we require the name tenth to be removed from it, applies when they emerge one after the other, for once he has called the certain tenth “tenth,” the eleventh is not sacred.
gershom:b20.1: But at the same time: when they emerge together and he called both of them tenth, [the eleventh] is sacred.
gershom:b21.1: Is it not to include at the same time? That the eleventh is not sacred then either.
rashi:b13.1: To include where the tenth emerged and he did not speak: for this silence does not count as removal unless he removed it explicitly and called it ninth.
gershom:b22.1: No, to include where the tenth emerged alone and he did not speak: he did not call it tenth, and afterward the eleventh emerged and he called it tenth; the eleventh is not sanctified, since the name tenth did not leave [the tenth], for the tenth is sacred of its own accord. But at the same time, both are sacred.
rashi:b14.1: Because if you do not say this: that at the same time it is sacred. And Rav Ashi, who challenged Rav Kahana, “But [the name] has not been removed,” etc., had not heard what we answered above: “This teaches us that [in every case where two emerge] at the same time,” etc.
rashi:b15.1: Here we are dealing with: [the baraita] that teaches “the tenth and eleventh are intermingled,” where we regard the eleventh as consecrated even though he called the tenth “tenth”: for example, where one went ahead, etc.
gershom:b23.1: Because if you do not say this, that which is taught, etc.: where one of them went ahead and put out its head and he called it eleventh before he called [anything] tenth, for then the name tenth was removed from the tenth.
rashi:b15.2: And called it eleventh: now the name tenth has been removed from it, since he did not call it tenth but eleventh; therefore, even though he then called both of them tenth, the eleventh is sacred. But where he had called it tenth at first, the eleventh would not be sacred, even at the same time. And we explain it as a case where he called it eleventh because, had he called it ninth, there would be no need to teach it, since that is certainly a removal; but regarding “eleventh,” Rabbi disagrees and says it is not a removal, as below, and it was necessary to teach us that it is a removal.
gershom:b24.1: And then it became intermingled, and at the moment of their actual emergence, neither went ahead of the other.
rashi:b17.1: And in accordance with whom: is our answer, that calling it eleventh counts as removal?
gershom:b25.1: And in accordance with whom: does he count this as removal, where he called it eleventh? Not in accordance with Rabbi.
rashi:b18.1: Where he has many animals: to tithe; now, when he counted the first ten and called the tenth “eleventh,” one can say that the name tenth was not removed from it by this, for what he meant by “eleventh [aḥad asar]” was “one tithe [ḥad issura],” that is, this is the first tithe.
gershom:b26.1: Where he has many animals: to tithe; for certainly when he calls the tenth “eleventh” he does not really mean eleventh, but he is calling it tenth.
gershom:b27.1: And he meant “one tithe”: that is, I have already counted one set of ten and have already separated one tithe of the tithes I must separate.
rashi:b18.2: But where he does not have more animals: than eleven, or twelve, or thirteen, or fourteen, or fifteen, one cannot say so, for it is not the way of the world to say “this is one tithe” unless one knows he will have many tithes. Therefore we say he really meant eleventh, and he removed the name tenth from it.
gershom:b28.1: Where he does not have many animals, only [nine]teen or fifteen: certainly when he calls it eleventh, even Rabbi agrees that this is a removal of the name tenth from it. And Rava’s statement, that at the same time both are sacred, does not stand.
rashi:b20.1: Two emerged at the tenth: this goes back, as the Master said, to Rava’s teaching above, who said: two emerged at the tenth and he called them tenth, the tenth and eleventh are intermingled with each other. And now the tanna explains: one [baraita] teaches that those two intermingled animals graze until they become blemished, and another teaches, etc.
gershom:b29.1: Two emerged at the tenth and he called them tenth.
rashi:b21.1: One may not bring sacrificial animals to disqualification: for if they were sacrificed, they would have to be eaten according to the stricter of the two, which requires that the breast and thigh be lifted from them and given to the priests; and since priests are few, and [that portion] is eaten only by priests, perhaps there will not be enough eaters for that breast and thigh, and they will be disqualified by being left over after two days and one night. And so he brings one of them, the tithe, to disqualification, for a tithe certainly does not require lifting the breast and thigh for the priests; rather, all of it is eaten by anyone, and many eaters are available for it, and it would never come to be disqualified by being left over. In tractate Zevaḥim, in the chapter Kol HaZevaḥim SheNitarevu (Zevaḥim 75b), we learn the dispute of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, as we learned: A guilt offering that became intermingled with a peace offering: Rabbi Shimon says both are slaughtered in the north and eaten according to the stricter of the two. They said to him: One may not bring sacrificial animals to disqualification.
gershom:b30.1: In accordance with the Rabbis, who say one may not bring sacrificial animals to disqualification: for the intermingled tenth and eleventh are a tithe and a peace offering; and if we say both are sacrificed, one must give breast and thigh from both because one may be the peace offering. Sometimes the priests have most of the offerings and cannot manage to eat this breast and thigh within their time, and it comes to disqualification [and] burning; whereas the tithe is fit to be eaten entirely by Israelites, except the sacrificial portions, and Israelites are many and can eat it within its time. Now we reduce its eating and give [part of it] to the priests, and it comes to disqualification. Therefore they graze until they become blemished, he redeems one of them, and both are eaten by the owners in their blemished state. And this is the dispute of the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon in tractate Zevaḥim, in the chapter Kol HaZevaḥim SheNitarevu BeḤatta’ot: a guilt offering that became intermingled with a peace offering, Rabbi Shimon says both are slaughtered in the north and eaten according to the stricter of the two, even though the peace offering comes to disqualification, as they cannot manage to eat it within the time of the guilt offering. They said to him: One may not bring sacrificial animals to disqualification.
